title: Water keeps you alive, so why do diamonds cost more?
body: Adam Smith described the puzzle in 1776: water is essential yet cheap, while diamonds are useless for survival yet expensive. Economists resolved it in the 1870s with marginal utility: prices reflect the value of one more unit, not of all units together. Water is usually plentiful, so an extra litre adds little, while diamonds are scarce, so one more is prized. Lost in a desert, you would rank them very differently.

slides.heading: How marginal utility sets a price

steps.label: Ask what one more unit is worth
Plenty of water: one more litre adds little
Few diamonds: one more is prized
Price follows the extra unit, not the total

slides.question: According to marginal utility, what does a price reflect?
options: The value of one more unit
The total usefulness of a good
The cost of digging it up
How badly you need it to survive
slides.explanation: Prices track the value of an extra unit. Water is usually plentiful, so one more litre adds little; diamonds are scarce, so one more is prized.

slides.clue: Economists’ word for the value of one more unit: ___ utility
slides.detail: From the Latin margo, an edge: what matters is the value at the edge of what you already have, which is what prices track.
